latest_release.name: v1.2.0 — the main path, rebuilt and tested
latest_release.body:
**The story skills are rebuilt around shared helper scripts, a read guard stops whole-file reads of large design docs, the engine references move to Godot 4.7 and Unreal Engine 5.8, and no skill pre-approves every shell command any more.** A minor release after 1.1.3.

### Highlights

- **The main path is rebuilt.** `/start`, `/create-stories`, `/story-readiness`, `/create-epics`, `/dev-story` and `/story-done` follow Anthropic's skill-authoring guidance: shorter, with rarely used branches in `references/` and fixed steps handed to helper scripts, so the same question gets the same answer each time. `/start` works out the rigor from what you describe and shows it on one card. `/create-stories` proposes an `S`, `M` or `L` estimate for each story.
- **Stories list their files, and evidence knows when its code changed.** The new story template has a `## Files` section: `/create-stories` plans it, `/dev-story` fills it and `/story-done` checks scope against it. `/dev-story` stamps a story's screenshots with the files they prove, and `/story-done` names any that changed since (#135, proposed by @jiangshoujie).
- **A read guard for large design docs.** A whole-file read of a doc over 40 KB under `design/`, `docs/architecture/` or `production/session-state/` is refused with the doc's headings, so the retry reads one section (#136, #140, suggested by @mamonbleau). It also ends the failed whole-ADR reads reported in #64 by @Shtruk. `features.read_guard: off` turns it off.
- **Session start says when a newer release is out.** One line, from at most one GitHub request a day made in the background; nothing about your project is sent. `updates.check: false` turns it off, and it is always off under CI.
- **Engine references for Godot 4.7 and Unreal Engine 5.8.** Unity stays on 6.3 LTS and lists 6.4 to 6.6 and the 6.7 beta. `/test-setup` writes current CI actions. Unreal 5.8 support was first proposed in #121 by @spirit986. Staying on Godot 4.6 or Unreal 5.7? Keep your current engine folder.
- **Helper scripts and registry checks.** New scripts in `.claude/scripts/` read story facts, ADR status, a Markdown section, the stage and the session checkpoint for the skills. More ship for you to run (bug counts, sprint arithmetic, tech-debt scores, flaky-test rates and others), each with `--help`. `registry.sh` validates the three registries and hands out IDs that are never reused.
- **Warnings for writes the skills never make**, such as replacing an existing `EPIC.md` or `project.godot`, crossing the prototype boundary or renumbering a registry entry. They warn and never block.
- **`/sprint-plan` checks that the sprint goal can be shown** and lists anything it needs that no story builds (based on an idea in #58 and #76 by @FreedomPortal).
- **Fixes**, among them: the commit check skips GDD copies in `design/gdd/` subfolders such as `archive/` (#133, reported by @mamonbleau); a repeated `modes:` key in `project.yaml` is merged and named instead of wiping the first; a multi-line value in `project.yaml` is read as text, never as settings; a stage never advances past a gate check that could not run; `/architecture-review` reuses a saved review only when nothing it read has changed, and `single-gdd` writes only that system; playtest records count as evidence from `production/qa/playtests/`; `/sprint-plan` never takes your answer to its QA-plan question as approval to write; in a Godot project, evidence screenshots under `production/` are no longer imported or packed into an export. The full list is in the CHANGELOG.

### Security

- **Skills pre-approve only the commands they run.** 34 skills had a bare `Bash` entry in `allowed-tools`, which let them run any shell command without asking in the default permission mode. Each now names its framework scripts and read-only commands. Anything else, including your `commands.test`, asks first: approve it once, or add `Bash(<your command> *)` to `.claude/settings.local.json`.

detail.readme_excerpt:
Claude Code Game Studios

Turn a single Claude Code session into a full game development studio.
49 agents. 74 skills. One coordinated AI team.

--- ## Why This Exists Building a game solo with AI is powerful — but a single chat session has no structure. No one stops you from hardcoding magic numbers, skipping design docs, or writing spaghetti code. There's no QA pass, no design review, no one asking "does this actually fit the game's vision?" **Claude Code Game Studios** solves this by giving your AI session the structure of a real studio. Instead of one general-purpose assistant, you get 49 specialized agents organized into a studio hierarchy — directors who guard the vision, department leads who own their domains, and specialists who do the hands-on work. Each agent has defined responsibilities, escalation paths, and quality gates. The result: you still make every decision, but now you have a team that asks the right questions, catches mistakes early, and keeps your project organized from first brainstorm to launch. --- ## Table of Contents - [What's Included](#whats-included) - [Studio Hierarchy](#studio-hierarchy) - [Slash Commands](#slash-commands) - [Does it produce games, or documents?](#does-it-produce-games-or-documents) - [Getting Started](#getting-started) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Upgrading](#upgrading) - [Project Structure](#project-structure) - [How It Works](#how-it-works) - [Design Philosophy](#design-philosophy) - [Customization](#customization) - [Platform Support](#platform-support) - [Community](#community) - [Supporting This Project](#supporting-this-project) - [License](#license) --- ## What's Included | Category | Count | Description | |----------|-------|-------------| | **Agents** | 49 | Specialized subagents acr
